title: Thirty-five years, 35 moments
lede: From a licensing plan to a courtroom auction, and a trademark quarrel 23 years later. Filter by thread.

events.title: Incorporated as SMSG, Inc.
events.text: The company is incorporated in California and begins operations in October. It takes the name The 3DO Company in September 1992.

events.title: Prototype shown at CES
events.text: Trip Hawkins demonstrates the system in Las Vegas and calls it the next consumer electronics standard. AT&T joins Time Warner and Matsushita as an investor. The first machines are expected to cost about $700.

events.title: NTG bought for $21.4M
events.text: 3DO buys the partnership that held a royalty agreement over its technology, for 1,840,000 shares and cash.

events.title: Goes public on Nasdaq
events.text: Shares begin trading under the symbol THDO. The offering raises $47.5M after costs.

events.title: The 3DO Multiplayer goes on sale
events.text: Matsushita sells the first machine under the Panasonic name at $699. The shares reach $47.75 during the month.

events.title: “Only four games”
events.text: A Matsushita vice president says the machine is selling poorly for lack of software. Colleagues answer that 40,000 have been shipped to the United States and more than 70% sold.

events.title: 3DO opens its own studio
events.text: After a disappointing Christmas the company begins making games itself, in competition with its licensees.

events.title: AT&T pulls out
events.text: AT&T says it will not make consumer products based on the 3DO design. Shareholders file securities suits the same month; they are dismissed in July 1995.

events.title: Hawkins leaves the EA chair
events.text: He steps down as chairman of Electronic Arts to concentrate on 3DO.

events.title: 300,000 machines
events.text: Matsushita says it has sold 200,000 in Japan and 100,000 elsewhere, short of an earlier forecast of half a million in the United States alone.

events.title: The $3 surcharge
events.text: Hawkins faxes developers a notice of an extra $3 fee per game to subsidise hardware makers. He cuts it to $1 for the rest of 1994.

events.title: Saturn and PlayStation launch in Japan
events.text: Sega sells out of 250,000 Saturns. Sony sells 100,000 PlayStations in two days from December 3.

events.title: Price down to $399
events.text: The list price has fallen from $699 in a year. The machine is in more than 6,000 stores. 3DO has about $21M of cash.

events.title: Sega and Sony reach the U.S.
events.text: Both launch 32-bit CD-ROM consoles in 1995. Sanyo and Creative Technology stop investing in their 3DO machines.

events.title: M2 for the PC
events.text: Hawkins says 3DO will make a version of its next-generation M2 technology for personal computers.

events.title: M2 licensed for $100M
events.text: Matsushita takes a perpetual, exclusive licence to the 64-bit M2 design for $100M upfront plus royalties.

events.title: Goldstar quits
events.text: LG Electronics (Goldstar) leaves the 32-bit business. Matsushita later says it will make no more 3DO Multiplayers.

events.title: New World Computing bought
events.text: 3DO pays about 1 million shares, and later about $5.0M in cash under a price guarantee, for the studio behind Might and Magic.

events.title: “An about-face”
events.text: 3DO says it will become a software company and sell or spin off its hardware group, cutting jobs from 450 to 300.

events.title: Hardware sold to Samsung
events.text: Samsung buys most of the hardware systems group for $20.0M. 3DO books a gain of $18.0M.

events.title: M2 console shelved
events.text: Matsushita’s president says the company has stopped developing the M2 console. On July 23 it returns about 3.2 million 3DO shares and 3DO gives up its M2 royalties.

events.title: Army Men carries the publisher
events.text: In the year to March 31, 1999 Army Men is 31% of revenue, Might and Magic 25% and BattleTanx 19%.

events.title: $46.4M raised
events.text: A second public offering of shares brings in about $46.4M after costs.

events.title: The peak
events.text: Revenue for the year to March 31, 2000 is $122.2M, up 154%. Net income is $0.2M.

events.title: Profit warning
events.text: 3DO says fiscal 2001 will lag estimates. Its chief financial officer plans to leave. The shares close at $5.59.

events.title: A $77.0M loss
events.text: The loss for the year to March 31, 2001. Sixty-nine jobs are cut.

events.title: “Substantial doubt”
events.text: Revenue falls to $53.7M with a $47.3M loss. The workforce has been cut by 160 and the annual report raises doubt about the company’s survival.

events.title: One-for-eight reverse split
events.text: Every eight shares become one.

events.title: Hawkins lends $3M
events.text: The chief executive lends the company $3,000,000, secured on all its assets. On December 27 he agrees to lend up to $8,000,000.

events.title: “Strategic options”
events.text: 3DO says March-quarter revenue was about $10.0M and that it is considering a sale or merger. It gave notice of a mass layoff on May 2.

events.title: Chapter 11
events.text: The 3DO Company and its California subsidiary file in the Northern District of California.

events.title: Delisted
events.text: Nasdaq removes the shares from the National Market.

events.title: The auction
events.text: The assets are sold in bankruptcy court for $4,585,000. Hawkins resigns from the board on August 29.

events.title: Registration revoked
events.text: The SEC revokes the registration of 3DO’s shares. It had filed no periodic report since the quarter ended December 31, 2002.

events.title: A revival, cancelled in a week
events.text: Empire Interactive says it has bought The 3DO Company trademark, then withdraws after Throwback Entertainment says it owns the 3DO mark.
